summary: This document changes the "Unassigned" number space in the IANA OSPFv3 Instance ID Address Family Values registry by splitting it in two. One half stays unassigned, managed via Standards Action, and the other is reserved for private use. It updates RFC 5838.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC divides the unassigned OSPFv3 Instance ID values into two ranges. Values 192–255 are reserved for private use, while 128–191 remain unassigned under a Standards Action process.

questions: what are ospfv3 private use instance ids
which ospfv3 instance ids are for private use
subtitle: Reserving part of the OSPFv3 Instance ID range for private use.

tldr.problem: Operators may need locally assigned OSPFv3 Instance IDs to distinguish particular applications, but the unassigned range had no private-use portion.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC designates 192–255 as Reserved for Private Use and makes the remaining unassigned values, 128–191, subject to Standards Action.
tldr.outcome: The update changes the OSPFv3 Instance ID Address Family Values registry and updates RFC 5838.

today: RFC 6969 is a Standards Track document that updates RFC 5838. It changes the allocation rules for the OSPFv3 Instance ID Address Family Values registry.

sections.title: Why a Private-Use Range Is Needed
sections.content: RFC 5838 defined the OSPFv3 Instance ID Address Family Values registry and left values 128–255 unassigned. RFC 6969 explains that some networks may need extra OSPFv3 instances to identify specific applications and need a range that operators can assign locally.
sections.plainLanguage: Some operators need local Instance IDs to identify applications in their networks. This RFC sets aside a range for that purpose.

sections.title: How the Registry Changes
sections.content: The updated registry reserves Instance IDs 192–255 for Private Use. The remaining unassigned values, 128–191, use the Standards Action registration procedure. The document updates the registry defined by RFC 5838.
sections.plainLanguage: Values 192–255 are reserved for private use. The smaller range from 128 to 191 remains unassigned and follows the Standards Action process.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that changing this registry does not introduce new security issues. It records a change to the IANA Instance ID registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says the registry change creates no new security issues.

sections.title: IANA Registry Update
sections.content: IANA modified the OSPFv3 Instance ID Address Family Values registry as described and removed the RFC 5838 reference from the modified ranges.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA updated the registry with the new ranges and removed the old reference for those entries.

references.text: Lindem, A., Mirtorabi, S., Roy, A., Barnes, M., and R. Aggarwal, "Support of Address Families in OSPFv3", RFC 5838, April 2010.
